messages.content: I added an index to my table but my query is still slow. What could be going on?

An index only helps if the query can actually use it, and there are several common ways to defeat one. Wrapping the indexed column in a function, such as WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@b.com' or WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2025, usually prevents a normal index lookup. A leading wildcard like LIKE '%smith' does the same, while LIKE 'smith%' can use the index. A type mismatch, such as comparing a text column to a number, can force a conversion on every row. The optimizer may also ignore the index on purpose when the query returns a large share of the table, since scanning can be cheaper than thousands of random lookups. And in a multi-column index, order matters: an index on (a, b) helps filters on a, or on a and b, but generally not on b alone. Rather than guessing further, run EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN ANALYZE) on the query and see whether it reports an index scan or a full table scan.
When should I use async/await in Python instead of threads?

Use async when you have many tasks that spend most of their time waiting on I/O, such as thousands of HTTP requests or open sockets. One thread running an event loop can switch between them cheaply while each one waits. Threads also handle I/O-bound work, but each one costs memory and the scheduling overhead grows with the count. Neither helps with CPU-bound work in standard CPython because of the global interpreter lock; for that, use multiprocessing or native extensions. The real cost of async is that it spreads through your code: a single blocking call such as requests.get or time.sleep inside a coroutine freezes the whole loop, so you need async-aware libraries like aiohttp or httpx. If you only have a handful of concurrent tasks, threads are usually simpler.
Why is appending to a Python list fast but inserting at the start slow?

A Python list is a contiguous array of references. Appending usually just writes into the next free slot, and when the array is full Python allocates a bigger one with spare room, so the occasional expensive resize averages out to constant time per append (amortized O(1)). Inserting at the front means shifting every existing element one position to make space, which is O(n). If you need fast operations at both ends, use collections.deque.
What actually happens between typing a URL and the page appearing?

Roughly in this order. The browser checks its caches and, if needed, asks a DNS resolver to turn the hostname into an IP address. It then opens a connection to that address (TCP, or QUIC for HTTP/3), and for https it runs a TLS handshake in which the server presents a certificate and both sides agree on encryption keys. The browser sends an HTTP request, and the server replies with a status code, headers and usually HTML. As the browser parses that HTML it discovers more resources, such as CSS, scripts and images, and fetches them too, often reusing the same connection. It then builds the DOM and styles, lays out the page, runs JavaScript and paints pixels, and this can continue for a while as scripts load more content. Many of these steps are skipped when things are cached, which is why a repeat visit feels faster.
What does LoRA actually change when you fine-tune a model?

It leaves the original weights frozen and trains small add-on matrices instead. For a chosen weight matrix W, LoRA learns two thin matrices, A and B, whose product has low rank r, and the layer then computes with W plus a scaled version of B times A (the scale is usually alpha divided by r). Because r is small, often between 8 and 64, you train a tiny fraction of the parameters, which cuts memory use enough to fit fine-tuning on a modest GPU. The adapter is also a small separate file that can be loaded, swapped, or merged back into the base weights. The trade-off is that a low-rank update has limited capacity, which is usually enough to shift style and behavior but less suited to teaching large amounts of new knowledge.
How can a vaccine train my immune system without making me sick?

A vaccine shows your immune system something that resembles the pathogen without being able to cause the full disease. Depending on the type, that might be a weakened live virus, an inactivated whole virus, a purified protein, or genetic instructions (mRNA or a viral vector) that make your own cells produce one harmless piece, such as a spike protein. Your immune system responds as it would to a real threat, producing antibodies and, importantly, memory B and T cells. If you meet the real pathogen later, those memory cells respond faster and more strongly, often before symptoms develop. The mild side effects some people get, like a sore arm or a day of feeling run down, come from the immune response itself, not from an infection.
Why is 1900 not a leap year but 2000 was?

The Gregorian rule is that a year is a leap year if it's divisible by 4, except years divisible by 100, which are not, unless they're also divisible by 400, which are. So 1900 fails (divisible by 100 but not 400) and 2000 passes (divisible by 400). The reason is that a solar year is about 365.2422 days, not 365.25, so adding a day every 4 years overcorrects by roughly 3 days every 400 years, and skipping three of every four century years fixes that.
My test for a rare disease came back positive and the test is 99% accurate. Does that mean there's a 99% chance I have it?

No, and this is a very common mix-up. Your chance of having the disease depends on how rare it is as well as on how good the test is. Suppose the disease affects 1 in 10,000 people and the test is right 99% of the time in both directions. Out of 10,000 people, about 1 has the disease and will almost certainly test positive, while about 100 of the 9,999 healthy people will also test positive by mistake. So of roughly 101 positive results, only about 1 is real, which is around 1 percent. The actual figure shifts a lot with the true prevalence and with your own risk factors, which is why a positive screening result is usually followed by a confirmatory test. If this is about a real result, ask your doctor what the test's positive predictive value is for someone in your situation.
When my close friend got promoted I smiled and congratulated her, but inside I felt sick with jealousy. Then I felt like a horrible person.

Feeling both is more common than people admit. You can be glad for someone and still feel the sting of comparison, and the two feelings don't cancel each other out. The jealousy isn't evidence that you're a horrible person; what you did with it, which was to congratulate her sincerely, is the part that counts morally. It's more useful to ask what the jealousy is about. Sometimes it points at something you want for yourself, like recognition or a change of role, and sometimes it's closer to a fear that her gain lowers your standing, which is a different problem and worth checking against reality. Those lead to different actions. The guilt on top of the envy adds nothing, so notice it and let it go.
I keep saying I'll start my own business once I have enough savings. I've been saying it for three years. Am I lying to myself?

Maybe, maybe not, and one test can tell you: have you ever named the amount? If 'enough' is a specific number, such as six months of expenses, and you're visibly moving toward it, then waiting is a plan. If the number has risen each time you got close, or you've never defined it, then 'enough' may be working as a way to postpone a decision without having to say no. There's another possibility worth considering: that part of you likes the idea of the business more than the business itself, which is a legitimate discovery, not a failure. Write down the exact figure and date, and pick one small test you can run now with little money, such as selling to a single customer. What happens when you try that will tell you more than another year of saving.
Since I graduated I feel weirdly lost. I don't know who I am if I'm not a student.

That makes sense. For years your days had structure, a clear measure of progress, and an answer to 'what do you do?' that people understood. Losing all three at once can feel like losing yourself, even though what you lost was a role. It helps to separate the two. A role is something you do; who you are is closer to what you care about, how you treat people and what you're curious about, and none of that ended at graduation. In practice, the gap tends to fill with new structure: a routine, a project with milestones, a group you belong to. Which of those do you miss most?
Why do I lie awake at 3am replaying embarrassing things I said years ago?

At 3am there are no distractions, and tiredness weakens your ability to keep things in perspective, so the mind goes through its stored material and tends to pick whatever feels unresolved or socially costly. Embarrassing memories get chosen partly because standing among other people matters a great deal to us, and partly because you remember your own slip in vivid detail while others forgot it within days, being busy worrying about their own. None of this proves that anything is wrong with you. If it happens often, keep a notepad by the bed and write one line about the memory, then get up and do something dull for fifteen minutes instead of lying there arguing with it. If it's frequent and wearing you down, a doctor or therapist can look at your sleep and anxiety more carefully than I can.
I got a chance to work abroad but the thought of leaving my parents makes me feel sick. Every week I decide the opposite.

Flip-flopping every week often means both options carry something you value, and each time you imagine one choice, the cost of the other gets louder. So it may help to stop asking which choice is right and ask what each one protects. Going protects growth and independence; staying protects closeness and your sense of duty. Neither is silly. Then check some facts you may currently be guessing at: how your parents actually feel about it, since they might surprise you, how often you could visit, how long the job lasts, and whether the move can be reversed. You could also try treating one option as decided for two days and notice whether you feel relief or dread. It isn't conclusive, but it's more informative than another round of arguing in your head.
I haven't opened my bank app in two months. I'm sure it's fine.

'I'm sure it's fine' is carrying a lot of weight there, since you can't really be sure about something you've avoided looking at. People often avoid checking when part of them suspects the number will be unpleasant, because not looking keeps the bad news hypothetical. But it doesn't stay hypothetical: fees, forgotten subscriptions and a low balance still happen whether or not you look. The effort required is small compared with the worry. Open it, check the balance and the last two months of transactions, and do nothing else for now. If it's fine, you've bought peace for a minute's work; if it isn't, it's much easier to fix in month three than in month six.
People tell me I'm defensive but honestly I think they just criticize me unfairly.

Both could be true, so the question is how to find out which. One useful check is whether the pattern shows up with different people. If it's one difficult boss, that points to them; if a manager, a partner and a friend all say something similar, one common factor is you. Another is what happens in the first few seconds after criticism. If you notice an urge to explain or counter before you've fully heard it, that is what others may call defensiveness, even when your point is correct. You could run a small experiment: when someone criticizes you, repeat back what they said and ask one question before you respond. You can still disagree afterward, but you'll know whether the criticism was fair instead of reacting to how it felt.
Why do I keep arguing even after I realize halfway that I'm wrong?

Because by then the argument is often no longer about the topic. Once you've defended a position out loud, conceding feels like losing standing, and for many people being wrong feels like a verdict on their competence instead of a fact about one claim. There's also momentum: stopping means admitting that the last few minutes were wasted. A way out is to make retreating cheaper. Phrases like 'Hold on, you've got a point' or 'I need to think about that' let you change your mind without a dramatic surrender, and most people respond well to them. Over time you may find that conceding early earns more respect than winning late.
A colleague I like is padding his expense reports by small amounts. Should I report him?

Real values are pulling against each other here. Against reporting: loyalty, proportion (small sums, a person's career at stake), and the chance that you're misreading something. For reporting: the money is still dishonest, colleagues who follow the rules are quietly disadvantaged, and tolerated habits tend to grow. A middle path is often available and morally meaningful. First confirm what you've actually seen, then speak to him directly, since small habits sometimes stop when someone says 'I noticed.' If it continues or gets worse, silence starts to look like participation, and escalating becomes harder to avoid, especially if your role gives you any responsibility over those reports. Not everyone would draw the line in the same place, but I'd be wary of any answer that treats this as either trivial or a betrayal.
Is it selfish to have children when the world has so much suffering and the climate is getting worse?

People of good conscience disagree on this. The case for hesitation: a child adds to resource use, brings a risk of suffering that they didn't choose, and the future does look uncertain. The case against calling it selfish: parents give a child a chance at a life that most people find worth living despite hardship, hope and effort are part of how a society continues, and humans have raised children through wars and plagues. The word selfish may also be doing too much work, because motives for wanting children are mixed, as with most major choices, and mixed motives don't make a choice wrong. On the climate argument, an individual's carbon footprint depends heavily on how a family lives and on policy changes, so it's less decisive than it sounds, though not trivial. Underneath all this is a question philosophy hasn't settled, about whether bringing someone into existence can harm or benefit them. I think the decision deserves to be treated as a serious one instead of being given a verdict.
Do I have to forgive someone who never apologized?

No. Forgiveness isn't something you owe; it's a choice, and for many people it follows repentance. But two things often get tangled together. One is forgiveness in the sense of releasing the grudge so it stops occupying your mind, which you can do privately and which doesn't need the other person's cooperation. The other is reconciliation, or trust, which does depend on them changing. You can let go of the first without offering the second. Some thinkers argue that forgiving without any acknowledgment from the wrongdoer cheapens the wrong; others argue that holding on mostly harms the one who holds on. Both have a point, and you don't have to settle it today.
Is it wrong to buy myself nice things while people are starving?

If you take the argument seriously, it's hard to dismiss. A modest sum can do a great deal for someone in extreme poverty, and nothing obvious makes a stranger's need count for less because of distance. Peter Singer's reasoning leads to a demanding conclusion that very few people, including most who accept it, live up to. On the other side, people argue that morality can't require total self-sacrifice, that we have special obligations to family and to our own projects, and that a life without any pleasure may be unsustainable and not what ethics is for. Most people settle somewhere in between, such as giving a fixed percentage consistently and enjoying the rest without guilt. That compromise isn't philosophically tidy, but it's honest about the tension. If the question bothers you, it may be a sign to choose a number deliberately so it stops hovering over every purchase.
Is it ever okay to break a promise to a friend in order to help someone else?

Yes, in many cases, but it isn't free. Most ethical views allow a serious need to override a promise, especially when the stakes for the other person are large compared with the inconvenience to your friend and you genuinely can't do both. A promise isn't meaningless, though: your friend arranged things around you, and the reliability of promises is what makes them worth anything. So a few things matter. How severe is the other need? Could someone else meet it? Can you reduce the damage to your friend by telling him early, finding a replacement, or making it up to him? Breaking a promise to drive someone to a hospital is different from breaking it for a better party. And tell him directly instead of just not showing up.
A judge hears a case of a man who stole food to feed his kids. Should he give a lighter sentence?

Two things we value are in conflict here: equal application of the law, and mercy that responds to circumstances. If judges sentence by sympathy, the law becomes unpredictable and may favor defendants who tell better stories. If they ignore circumstances, the law becomes mechanical and can punish desperation as harshly as greed. Most legal systems try to hold both by letting judges weigh motive and necessity at sentencing while still treating the act as an offense, though necessity rarely works as a full defense for ordinary theft. There's a further question about whether the fault lies with the individual or with failures of support around him. The judge can't fix that, but a lenient sentence can respond to it. In the case described I'd lean toward leniency within the law, while recognizing the argument that each exception weakens the rule.
Should parents be allowed to read their teenager's messages?

It depends on the age, the reason, and whether the teenager knows. The conflict is between a parent's responsibility to protect a minor from real dangers like predators, self-harm and drug dealing, and a teenager's need for privacy, which is part of how they develop independence and trust. Secret monitoring can protect in the short term, but if it's discovered it often damages trust and teaches kids to hide things better. Open arrangements, such as agreed rules about apps or occasional checks the teen knows about, are easier to defend. Specific evidence of danger changes the calculation: a parent who has found signs of serious risk has a stronger case for looking than one who is simply anxious. So instead of a yes or no, I'd ask what the parent is trying to prevent and whether a conversation could achieve it at lower cost.
Is it fair to judge historical figures by today's moral standards?

There are two opposite mistakes. One is presentism: condemning people for not sharing views that nobody around them held, as if they'd had access to our moral education. The other is treating 'everyone did it' as an excuse, when there were always dissenters, including the people being harmed, who knew it was wrong and said so. A reasonable approach is to separate explanation from evaluation. We can explain how someone came to hold their views and still say the views were wrong and the actions did harm. It's also worth asking whether the person had access to the arguments against their position and ignored them, because that makes blame stronger. Some will find this too lenient and others too harsh, and the disagreement itself shows how hard it is to apply moral standards across time.
How long do I boil an egg for a runny yolk?
About 6 to 7 minutes for a large egg lowered into already boiling water, then straight into cold water to stop the cooking. Closer to 6 gives a properly liquid yolk, and 7 gives a jammy one.
How do I politely end a phone call with someone who never stops talking?

Wait for a natural pause and give a reason plus a warm sign-off, instead of just hinting: 'I have to run, but it was great hearing from you. Let's talk again soon.' If they start a new topic, interrupt kindly: 'Sorry to cut in, I've got to go.' It feels rude, but most people take it fine, and a clear ending is kinder than growing visibly distracted while pretending to listen.
Should I wait before texting back so I don't look too eager?

Mostly no. Answer when you'd normally answer. Deliberate delays turn a conversation into a game, and people worth talking to usually care more about the reply than the timing. If you're busy, take your time; if you're not, reply.
how do i get red wine out of a cotton shirt

Act quickly and blot, don't rub, with a clean cloth to lift as much as you can. Rinse from the back of the fabric with cold water, then work in a little dish soap. For a stubborn mark on white cotton, equal parts dish soap and hydrogen peroxide can help, but test it on a hidden spot first because peroxide can lighten colored fabric. Rinse and wash as usual, and check that the stain is gone before using a dryer, because heat sets it permanently. Salt or baking soda on a fresh stain can help absorb it, though they aren't essential.
Is it weird to eat at a restaurant alone?

Not weird, just less common than it feels from the inside. Staff see solo diners all the time, and most other customers are absorbed in their own tables. Bring a book if it makes you more comfortable, or sit at the counter or bar if there is one. A table for one is also usually easy to get without a reservation.
What should I name my cat? She's grey and judges everything I do.

A cat with that attitude deserves a name with some gravity. Magistrate, Inspector, Verdict, or Duchess if she sits like she owns the house. For something quieter, Ash or Smoke suits the color. Try a few out loud and watch her reaction, though with cats the acceptance is usually silent.
I've been exhausted for weeks, work is crushing me and everything feels kind of pointless. I don't even know what I'm asking.

That sounds like a heavy stretch, and you don't need a precise question to talk about it. Weeks of exhaustion together with a feeling that nothing matters is worth taking seriously, whatever the cause. It could be workload, sleep, something else going on in your life, or a mix, and I can't tell which from here. Two practical things. If you can, look at what at work is actually draining you, such as the hours, a specific person, or having no say in anything, because that shows you what can change. And if the flat, pointless feeling continues for another couple of weeks or gets heavier, please see a doctor, because low mood and exhaustion have treatable causes and shouldn't just be endured. Is there someone around you who knows how bad it's been?
My friend told me she has cancer and I froze. I said 'oh no' and then changed the subject. I feel terrible.

Freezing is a very common reaction. Most people have no script for that moment, and it doesn't mean you don't care. You can still put it right, and sooner is better. Send her a message or call: 'I've been thinking about what you told me, and I'm sorry I didn't say more at the time. I'm here, and I'd like to hear how you're doing whenever you want to talk.' Then follow her lead on how much she wants to share. Avoid advice about treatments, or stories about other people's cases, unless she asks. Specific offers help more than 'let me know if you need anything', such as bringing a meal, driving her to an appointment, or just sitting with her.
My mum calls five times a day and gets really upset if I don't answer. I love her but it's suffocating.

You can love her and still need room; the two don't conflict. It may help to replace the unpredictable calls with something predictable, so she doesn't feel dropped and you don't feel hunted. For example, tell her you'll call every day at a set time, say 7 pm, and that if you miss a call during the day you'll text that you're busy and will ring at that time. Say it kindly and in advance, not in the moment when you're irritated: 'I want to talk to you every day, and I can give you real attention at 7, not in between meetings.' If she's anxious or lonely, the schedule needs to feel like more connection, not less. Expect it to take a few weeks and for her to be a bit upset at first.
I didn't get the job I really wanted. I thought the interview went well. I feel crushed.

That's a real disappointment, especially after you'd put hope into it. Give yourself a little time to feel it before you start looking for lessons. When you're ready, it's reasonable to email the recruiter and ask for brief feedback. Some will give it and some won't, and the reason may have nothing to do with you, such as an internal candidate or a budget change. An interview feeling good is also a weak predictor of the outcome, so the gap between how it felt and what happened isn't proof that you misjudged yourself. In the meantime, keep any other applications moving, since one rejection shouldn't mean everything stops.
I was really mean to my little brother yesterday and he's not talking to me. I feel awful.

Feeling awful shows you understand that it mattered to him, which is a good starting point. The most useful thing now is a straightforward apology with no 'but' in it. Tell him what you did, that it was wrong, and that you're sorry: 'I shouldn't have said those things. I was out of line and I'm sorry.' Don't ask him to forgive you right away, and don't explain how stressed you were; if he's hurt, he may need a few days. Then show it in how you treat him afterward. If he stays silent for a while, that doesn't mean the apology failed.
I store user passwords hashed with MD5. That's secure enough, right?

No, MD5 is a poor choice for passwords. It's designed to be fast, which is the opposite of what you want: attackers can test billions of guesses per second on ordinary graphics cards, and MD5 hashes of common passwords are cracked almost instantly, often just by lookup tables. Passwords should be stored with a slow, salted algorithm built for the purpose, such as bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2.
It's just a small hobby site with like 50 users, nobody's going to bother attacking it.

That's a fair point about being a target, and the stakes are lower for a hobby site. Two things still apply, though. Attacks are often automated and don't care about size, and the bigger risk is password reuse: if your 50 users use the same password elsewhere, a leak from your site could expose their email or bank accounts. Also, switching costs almost nothing. In Python it's a couple of lines with bcrypt or argon2-cffi, or your framework's built-in hasher, and you get far better protection for the same effort. For existing users, you can re-hash each password with the new algorithm the next time they log in.
My coworker is nice to everyone but barely talks to me. I think she hates me.

That could be true, but it's one of several possible explanations, and 'hates me' is the most painful of them, so it's worth checking before you accept it. She might be shy with people she doesn't know well, or busy, or on a different working rhythm. Has she done anything specific, like excluding you from something, or is it mainly less warmth than you see her giving others?
Mostly less warmth. Actually she invited me to the team lunch last week, I just didn't go because I assumed she was being polite.

That changes the picture quite a bit. Someone who dislikes you rarely invites you to lunch, so the invitation is more evidence for 'she's reserved' than for 'she hates me', and it's possible your decline read to her as a sign that you didn't want to be included. You don't need to make a big deal of it. Next time something comes up, say yes, or mention that you'd like to join the next one. Small, low-pressure contact usually does more than trying to decode her.
Is it wrong to be rich when so many people are poor?

Not by itself. What's usually questioned isn't the amount of money but how it was made and what is done with it. Wealth gained through exploitation or fraud is a problem, while wealth gained by producing something people value, or by good luck, is different. Then there's the question of obligation: many ethical views say that someone with far more than they need has some duty to help others, even if they disagree about how much. Others stress that people shouldn't be forced to give away what they've earned. So the debate is less about being rich than about what, if anything, the rich owe.
But what if I earned all of it myself through hard work? Why do I owe anyone anything?

If you earned it fairly, you have a strong claim to it, and many philosophers would agree that you owe no one an apology for success. The pushback tends to come in two forms. One is about luck: even hard workers benefit from things they didn't earn, like health, education, the country they were born in and the people who helped them, so 'all by myself' is rarely fully accurate. The other is about need: even if the money is entirely yours, you might think a person in dire need has a claim on part of your surplus. You can reject either argument, but I think the first is harder to dismiss. Where you land on the second is a matter of values, and reasonable people differ.
What laptop should I buy?

It depends mainly on what you'll do with it and what you can spend. A laptop for browsing and documents is very different from one for programming or video editing. What will you mainly use it for, and what's your budget?
Coding mostly, some video editing for YouTube. Budget around ₹80,000. I'd like it to last 4 years.

For that use and budget, prioritize specs over brand. Aim for 16 GB of RAM, since coding tools and editing software both use a lot, and ideally a model where the RAM can be upgraded later. Get a 512 GB SSD, a recent mid-range processor from the Ryzen 5/7 or Core i5/i7 H-series range for sustained performance, and a good screen, because you'll look at it for hours. A dedicated GPU helps with editing, but at this budget a strong integrated one is acceptable if the rest is good; if you can find a modest dedicated GPU, video export will be faster. Battery life and keyboard matter on a four-year machine, so read reviews that actually test them, and check warranty and service availability in your city. Models change quickly, so compare two or three current ones against this list instead of buying on a single recommendation.
I think I'm going to quit my master's. I feel like a total failure.

That sounds painful, and I'd separate two things: the decision to quit and the feeling of failure. They don't necessarily come together. Plenty of people leave programs for sound reasons, and plenty of others feel like failures while doing well. What's been happening that's making you want to leave?
I just don't enjoy it anymore. My parents paid so much though, they'll be devastated.

The guilt about the money is understandable, and it's worth treating separately, because it can push you in either direction: staying out of guilt can be as much a trap as leaving out of discouragement. Since you say you don't enjoy it, I'd try to work out whether the problem is the subject, this particular program or supervisor, or just a rough semester. A conversation with an advisor about taking leave or changing focus is possible before you make anything final. When you talk to your parents, they may take it better than you expect if you arrive with a plan instead of a surprise. Whatever you decide, the money already spent is gone either way; the question is what you want the next few years to be.
